questions.stem: A 22-year-old soldier is brought in by fellow squad-mates after a 3 kms ruck march in which the patient collapsed at mile. The squad-mates are concerned because the patient has been talking nonsensically and will not answer their questions appropriately. Rectal temperature shows 104.4°F. You immediately begin implementing cooling measures and place the patient in water immersion. At what temperature do you remove the patient from the water immersion?
questions.stemHtml: A 22-year-old soldier is brought in by fellow squad-mates after a 3 kms ruck march in which the patient collapsed at mile. The squad-mates are concerned because the patient has been talking nonsensically and will not answer their questions appropriately. Rectal temperature shows 104.4°F. You immediately begin implementing cooling measures and place the patient in water immersion. At what temperature do you remove the patient from the water immersion?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - 101.5°F - 102.0°F: High heat and humidity can impair the body's ability to dissipate heat through evaporation, convection, conduction, and radiation. Exertional heat illness is the result of an inability to maintain adequate cardiac output because of strenuous physical exercise and environmental heat stress. Rapid cooling is the most effective strategy to prevent ongoing morbidity and mortality. When the rectal temperature reaches 101 to 102 degrees F, active cooling measures should be stopped. Ice water immersion is the ideal method of cooling, but tepid water will be helpful if cold water is unavailable. If a rectal temperature is not available, then the patient should be cooled until he begins to shiver. A typical rate of cooling with cold water immersion is 0.37 degrees F per minute. Incorrect Options: Option A, B and C - Active cooling should stop when the patient begins to shiver or the patient's temperature reaches 101.5 to 102 degrees Fahrenheit. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Correct Option D - 101.5°F - 102.0°F:

  • High heat and humidity can impair the body's ability to dissipate heat through evaporation, convection, conduction, and radiation.
  • Exertional heat illness is the result of an inability to maintain adequate cardiac output because of strenuous physical exercise and environmental heat stress.
  • Rapid cooling is the most effective strategy to prevent ongoing morbidity and mortality.
  • When the rectal temperature reaches 101 to 102 degrees F, active cooling measures should be stopped.
  • Ice water immersion is the ideal method of cooling, but tepid water will be helpful if cold water is unavailable.
  • If a rectal temperature is not available, then the patient should be cooled until he begins to shiver.
  • A typical rate of cooling with cold water immersion is 0.37 degrees F per minute.

Incorrect Options:

Option A, B and C - Active cooling should stop when the patient begins to shiver or the patient's temperature reaches 101.5 to 102 degrees Fahrenheit.

questions.stem: What type of necrosis is most likely observed in the brain biopsy of a patient with a brain abscess?
questions.stemHtml: What type of necrosis is most likely observed in the brain biopsy of a patient with a brain abscess?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Liquefactive necrosis: The clinical presentation and radiological findings described in the case are suggestive of a brain abscess, which is commonly associated with liquefactive necrosis. Liquefactive necrosis is a type of necrosis where tissue architecture is completely lost, and the affected area transforms into a fluid-filled space due to the action of hydrolytic enzymes, particularly in the presence of neutrophils. This type of necrosis is often observed in bacterial or fungal infections, as well as in ischemic infarctions of the brain. In this case, the neutrophilic infiltrate seen in the histopathological examination of the brain biopsy is characteristic of liquefactive necrosis. The ring-enhancing lesion observed on MRI is a result of the accumulation of inflammatory cells and fluid at the border between the necrotic tissue and the surrounding healthy tissue. Incorrect Options: Option A - Coagulative necrosis: Coagulative necrosis is a type of necrosis commonly seen in ischemic injuries (In all organs except brain), such as in myocardial infarction. It is characterized by the preservation of the tissue architecture with coagulation of proteins, and enzymes, so blocks the proteolysis of the dead cells; resulting in a firm texture. Option C - Fibrinoid necrosis: Associated with the antigen - antibody reactions (immune complex deposition). Some examples are: Polyarteritis Nodosa (PAN) Rheumatic Heart Disease (RHD) SLE Malignant Hypertension (HTN Option D - Fat necrosis: Fat necrosis is often seen in adipose tissue after trauma or pancreatitis. It is characterized by the formation of chalky-white areas due to the saponification of fatty acids. @Neet_pg_bot

  • In this case, the neutrophilic infiltrate seen in the histopathological examination of the brain biopsy is characteristic of liquefactive necrosis. The ring-enhancing lesion observed on MRI is a result of the accumulation of inflammatory cells and fluid at the border between the necrotic tissue and the surrounding healthy tissue.

Incorrect Options:

Option A - Coagulative necrosis:

  • Coagulative necrosis is a type of necrosis commonly seen in ischemic injuries (In all organs except brain), such as in myocardial infarction. It is characterized by the preservation of the tissue architecture with coagulation of proteins, and enzymes, so blocks the proteolysis of the dead cells; resulting in a firm texture.

Option C - Fibrinoid necrosis:

Option D - Fat necrosis:

  • Fat necrosis is often seen in adipose tissue after trauma or pancreatitis. It is characterized by the formation of chalky-white areas due to the saponification of fatty acids.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the treatment of choice for managing gout with renal failure?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is the treatment of choice for managing gout with renal failure?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Febuxostat: Febuxostat is a xanthine oxidase inhibitor that reduces uric acid production and is considered a suitable alternative to allopurinol in patients with renal impairment. Unlike allopurinol, febuxostat does not require dose adjustment based on renal function. Therefore, it is the most appropriate drug of choice for managing gout in this patient with renal failure. Before initiating treatment with febuxostat, acute gout should be managed. The use of xanthine oxidase inhibitors is contraindicated during a gout flare-up due to the possibility of worsening of the acute condition. Information Summary Treatment initiation Start hypouricemic therapy when the patient's condition improves Tophi disappearance Continue therapy until tophi completely disappear Uric acid levels Maintain normal uric acid levels for 6 consecutive months Dietary considerations Limit non-vegetarian food and control purine intake Weight management Control weight to support management of gout symptoms Diuretic adjustment Adjust diuretic dosage or switch to calcium channel blockers, if necessary 24-hour urinary uric acid levels Evaluate levels to determine if the patient is an overproducer or under excretor of uric acid Incorrect Options: Option A - Allopurinol: Allopurinol is a commonly used medication for managing gout by reducing uric acid production. However, it is metabolized in the liver and excreted by the kidneys. In patients with renal failure, the dosage of allopurinol needs to be adjusted due to the increased risk of adverse effects and toxicity. Option B - Colchicine: Colchicine is an anti-inflammatory medication used for the treatment of acute gout attacks. However, it is primarily metabolized in the liver and eliminated by the kidneys. In patients with renal failure, colchicine can accumulate and lead to increased toxicity. Therefore, it is not the ideal choice in this scenario. Option C - Prednisone: Prednisone is a corticosteroid that can be used to manage acute gout attacks by reducing inflammation. It is not specifically contraindicated in patients with renal failure. However, it is not the drug of choice for long-term management of gout in these patients. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Correct Option D - Febuxostat:

  • Febuxostat is a xanthine oxidase inhibitor that reduces uric acid production and is considered a suitable alternative to allopurinol in patients with renal impairment. Unlike allopurinol, febuxostat does not require dose adjustment based on renal function.
  • Therefore, it is the most appropriate drug of choice for managing gout in this patient with renal failure.
  • Before initiating treatment with febuxostat, acute gout should be managed. The use of xanthine oxidase inhibitors is contraindicated during a gout flare-up due to the possibility of worsening of the acute condition. 

Information

Summary

Treatment initiation

Start hypouricemic therapy when the patient's condition improves

Tophi disappearance

Continue therapy until tophi completely disappear

Uric acid levels

Maintain normal uric acid levels for 6 consecutive months

Dietary considerations

Limit non-vegetarian food and control purine intake

Weight management

Control weight to support management of gout symptoms

Diuretic adjustment

Adjust diuretic dosage or switch to calcium channel blockers, if necessary

24-hour urinary uric acid levels

Evaluate levels to determine if the patient is an overproducer or under excretor of uric acid

Incorrect Options:

Option A - Allopurinol: Allopurinol is a commonly used medication for managing gout by reducing uric acid production. However, it is metabolized in the liver and excreted by the kidneys. In patients with renal failure, the dosage of allopurinol needs to be adjusted due to the increased risk of adverse effects and toxicity.

Option B - Colchicine: Colchicine is an anti-inflammatory medication used for the treatment of acute gout attacks. However, it is primarily metabolized in the liver and eliminated by the kidneys. In patients with renal failure, colchicine can accumulate and lead to increased toxicity. Therefore, it is not the ideal choice in this scenario.

Option C - Prednisone: Prednisone is a corticosteroid that can be used to manage acute gout attacks by reducing inflammation. It is not specifically contraindicated in patients with renal failure. However, it is not the drug of choice for long-term management of gout in these patients.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old G2P1A0 patient at 30 weeks gestation presents with complaints of vaginal spotting. She is admitted to a labor room for evaluation. Ultrasonography (USG) reveals a placenta covering a portion of the internal cervical opening. She currently shows no active vaginal bleeding. Cardiac tocography (CTG) shows a fetal heart rate of 130/bpm with no late or recurrent deacceleration. What is the next best step in the management of this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 29-year-old G2P1A0 patient at 30 weeks gestation presents with complaints of vaginal spotting. She is admitted to a labor room for evaluation. Ultrasonography (USG) reveals a placenta covering a portion of the internal cervical opening. She currently shows no active vaginal bleeding. Cardiac tocography (CTG) shows a fetal heart rate of 130/bpm with no late or recurrent deacceleration. What is the next best step in the management of this patient?

options.label: B
options.text: Resuscitation and observation in high risk ward

options.label: C
options.text: Amniocentesis to assess fetal lung maturity and plan delivery

options.label: D
options.text: Gentle cervical examination to assess dilatation and amnionic membrane status

questions.answerText: Resuscitation and observation in high risk ward
questions.solution: Correct Option: Option B: Resuscitation and observation in a high-risk ward The patient has placenta previa, as the USG shows the placenta covering a portion of the internal cervical opening. For the management of preterm placenta previa patients, the McAfee Johnson Regime is used ; the aim is to continue the pregnancy for fetal maturity without compromising maternal health. If the duration of pregnancy is <37 weeks, active vaginal bleeding is absent, and mother and fetal well-being are assured, then resuscitation and observation in a high-risk ward are expected. Steroid therapy is indicated when the duration of pregnancy is less than 34 weeks . Incorrect Options: Option A: Cesarean delivery C-section is not indicated at 30 weeks gestation in a patient with mild vaginal spotting. The fetus has a normal heart rate of 130 bpm ruling out any acidemia or low perfusion. It is more beneficial at this stage for the fetus to prolong pregnancy to allow time for fetal lungs to mature. Option C: Amniocentesis to assess fetal lung maturity and plan delivery Amniocentesis is indicated at certain times to assess fetal lung maturity by looking at the ratio of lecithin to sphingomyelin. An L/S ratio of 2.0-2.5 indicates fetal lung maturity. It is, however, not indicated in this patient as immediate delivery is not indicated, also at 30 weeks the lung maturity is most likely not reached, thus an invasive procedure like amniocentesis can be avoided Option D: Gentle cervical examination to assess dilatation and amnionic membrane status The cervical examination is contraindicated in placenta previa patients until the location of the placenta has been determined with transvaginal ultrasound (USG). It may cause bleeding, and at times it can cause sudden massive bleeding. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Correct Option:

Option B: Resuscitation and observation in a high-risk ward

  • The patient has placenta previa, as the USG shows the placenta covering a portion of the internal cervical opening.
  • For the management of preterm placenta previa patients, the McAfee Johnson Regime is used; the aim is to continue the pregnancy for fetal maturity without compromising maternal health.
  • If the duration of pregnancy is <37 weeks, active vaginal bleeding is absent, and mother and fetal well-being are assured, then resuscitation and observation in a high-risk ward are expected.
  • Steroid therapy is indicated when the duration of pregnancy is less than 34 weeks.

Incorrect Options:

Option A:  Cesarean delivery

  • C-section is not indicated at 30 weeks gestation in a patient with mild vaginal spotting.
  • The fetus has a normal heart rate of 130 bpm ruling out any acidemia or low perfusion.
  • It is more beneficial at this stage for the fetus to prolong pregnancy to allow time for fetal lungs to mature.

Option C: Amniocentesis to assess fetal lung maturity and plan delivery

  • Amniocentesis is indicated at certain times to assess fetal lung maturity by looking at the ratio of lecithin to sphingomyelin.
  • An L/S ratio of 2.0-2.5 indicates fetal lung maturity.
  • It is, however, not indicated in this patient as immediate delivery is not indicated, also at 30 weeks the lung maturity is most likely not reached, thus an invasive procedure like amniocentesis can be avoided

Option D: Gentle cervical examination to assess dilatation and amnionic membrane status

  • The cervical examination is contraindicated in placenta previa patients until the location of the placenta has been determined with transvaginal ultrasound (USG).
  • It may cause bleeding, and at times it can cause sudden massive bleeding.

questions.stem: What is the mechanism of action of the recently added diabetes medication that may exacerbate congestive heart failure symptoms in a male with a history of CHF?
questions.stemHtml: What is the mechanism of action of the recently added diabetes medication that may exacerbate congestive heart failure symptoms in a male with a history of CHF?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - PPAR gamma upregulation: In this case, the patient with a history of congestive heart failure (CHF) and diabetes mellitus is experiencing worsening symptoms of CHF since starting a new medication for diabetes management. The medication belongs to a class of drugs known as thiazolidinediones (pioglitazone and rosiglitazone), which bind to the PPAR gamma (peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma). Agonists of this receptor regulate a large number of genes, promote adipocyte differentiation, and increase peripheral utilization of glucose by increasing GLUT 4 Receptors on muscle/adipose tissue, responsible for decreasing insulin resistance. However, PPAR GAMMA inhibitors have been associated with several adverse effects, including fluid retention and worsening heart failure symptoms in patients with pre-existing cardiovascular conditions such as CHF. These drugs can cause sodium and water retention, leading to increased fluid volume and exacerbation of CHF symptoms. Incorrect Options : Option A and B: Beta-adrenergic receptor antagonists and Angiotensin-converting enzymes are commonly used medications for the management of CHF and cardiovascular conditions. They have different mechanisms of action and are not typically associated with worsening CHF symptoms in patients with appropriate indications and monitoring. Option D - GLP-1 agonists: These are a class of medications used for the management of diabetes. They work by stimulating the GLP-1 receptors to increase insulin secretion, decrease glucagon secretion, and delay gastric emptying. GLP-1 agonists have shown cardiovascular benefits and are not typically associated with worsening CHF symptoms. @Neet_pg_bot

  • However, PPAR GAMMA inhibitors have been associated with several adverse effects, including fluid retention and worsening heart failure symptoms in patients with pre-existing cardiovascular conditions such as CHF. Option A and B: Beta-adrenergic receptor antagonists and Angiotensin-converting enzymes are commonly used medications for the management of CHF and cardiovascular conditions. questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy is brought into the ER by his mother visibly upset, with the complaint that the child had been playing at home when he somehow got into a drawer that held a container of Super Glue (cyanoacrylate). Apparently he opened it up and squirted out the glue, which got onto his hands as well as into his left eye. His fingers are now glued together and his left eye is glued shut. The boy is upset but does not appear in any distress. His vitals in the ER are BP 90/60, HR 100, RR 20, Temp 98.9, Sat 99% on RA. What should be done for this patient?

options.label: A

options.label: B

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Apply erythromycin eye ointment to the eye to slowly loosen the glue and then gently pry open the lid. Bacitracin ointment or mineral oil can be applied to the fingers for the same purpose. Have him follow up with ophthalmology in a day to make sure all the glue is gone from his eye: Cyanoacylate (Crazy or Super Glue) is also used in surgical wound adhesives. It is nontoxic, however, it can cause problems by sticking together lips, fingers, or eyelids. To remove the glue, an oil-based material is needed such as erythromycin or Bacitracin ointment or mineral oil . For eyes that are stuck together, erythromycin eye ointment is effective and very safe - this applies to glue stuck to the cornea as well as the lids. Follow-up with an eye doctor can be done in a day or two. Incorrect Options: Option A - The boy should be immediately sent to the ophthalmologist's office for surgical debridement: This option suggests sending the child directly to an ophthalmologist for surgical debridement. Surgical debridement involves removing tissue that may have been damaged or glued together by the cyanoacrylate glue. While surgical debridement may be necessary in some cases of severe eye injury, it is not typically the first-line approach for a child who accidentally gets Super Glue in their eye. Surgical interventions should be considered only if less invasive methods are unsuccessful or if there is evidence of significant eye damage. In this case, it's important to start with less invasive and less risky measures. Option C - Irrigate the eye with warm water and soak the stuck fingers in Betadine to loosen the glue: This option suggests irrigating the eye with warm water and soaking the glued fingers in Betadine to loosen the glue. While irrigation may be appropriate for some chemical exposures, it may not be the best approach for cyanoacrylate glue, as this type of glue hardens upon exposure to water. Irrigating the eye in this case could potentially worsen the situation and create further complications. It is not recommended to use water or Betadine to address cyanoacrylate glue in the eye or on the skin. Option D - Gently pry open the eyelid and fingers with traction: This option suggests attempting to gently pry open the eyelid and fingers with traction. This approach is not recommended, especially when dealing with a child's eye. Attempting to forcibly open the eyelid can cause damage to the delicate eye structures, and prying open glued fingers could result in injury as well. This approach may lead to more harm than good and should be avoided. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy presents with right knee pain and a limp. He has no history of trauma. His hip is abducted and externally rotated,with exacerbation of pain with internal rotation. What is the most likely cause of this symptom?
questions.stemHtml: A 5-year-old boy presents with right knee pain and a limp. He has no history of trauma. His hip is abducted and externally rotated,with exacerbation of pain  with internal rotation. What is the most likely cause of this symptom?
questions.solution: Correct Option C- Transient synovitis: Transient synovitis and septic arthritis are the most common causes of atraumatic hip pain in children . Transient synovitis usually occurs in children between the ages of 3 and 8 years of age, most often in boys. Children typically have had symptoms for one to three days at presentation and will demonstrate an antalgic gait with an abducted and externally rotated hip at rest. Pain is exacerbated with internal rotation of the hip, although pain with motion is less severe than in children with septic arthritis of the hip. Referred pain to the knee may be the only complaint , so careful inspection of the hip is mandatory in all patients with isolated knee pain. Referred pain from the hip to knee is usually a dull pain that is located anteriorly and does not localize to bone or soft tissue. Examination of the knee is usually normal. The hip exam typically demonstrates a limited range of motion with pain. Serious causes of hip pain must be excluded, including septic arthritis, fracture, slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE), and Legg-Calve-Perthes disease. Patients with transient synovitis rarely have a fever Management of transient synovitis is purely supportive and includes rest and NSAIDs. Incorrect Options: Option A- Femoral neck fracture: Hip fracture in a paediatric patient is suggested by high-force trauma, and severe tenderness is common. Option B- Osteogenesis imperfecta: Osteogenesis imperfecta is a rare disease that causes problems in bone synthesis due to collagen defects. Frequent fractures are common, and a physical examination may demonstrate blue sclerae, deafness, and ligamentous laxity. Subclinical cases may be more common than previously recognized. Option D- Slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE): SCFE occurs when the femoral epiphysis slips off the metaphysis, usually in adolescents. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 28-year-old male is brought to the emergency department by his friends. They report finding him unconscious at home. On examination, the patient's breathing is shallow, and his pupils are pinpoint. He is unresponsive and exhibits signs of hypothermia and hypotension. What is the most likely diagnosis, and what is the appropriate treatment for this condition?
questions.stemHtml: A 28-year-old male is brought to the emergency department by his friends. They report finding him unconscious at home. On examination, the patient's breathing is shallow, and his pupils are pinpoint. He is unresponsive and exhibits signs of hypothermia and hypotension. What is the most likely diagnosis, and what is the appropriate treatment for this condition?
questions.solution: Correct Option B: Opioid intoxication; administer IV naloxone. The clinical presentation of unconsciousness, shallow breathing, pinpoint pupils (miosis), hypothermia, and hypotension is highly suggestive of opioid intoxication. Opioids, such as heroin or prescription pain medications, can cause respiratory depression, CNS depression leading to coma, and pupillary constriction. The appropriate treatment for opioid intoxication is IV naloxone, an opioid antagonist. Naloxone acts quickly to reverse the effects of opioids by displacing them from their receptors. It can rapidly restore normal respiration and improve consciousness. Incorrect Options: Option A - Alcohol intoxication; administer IV lorazepam: It is incorrect as alcohol intoxication typically presents with different symptoms such as unsteady gait, slurred speech, and disinhibition. The treatment for alcohol intoxication does not involve IV lorazepam but rather supportive care. Option C - Benzodiazepine overdose; administer IV flumazenil: It is incorrect as benzodiazepine overdose presents with symptoms like excessive sedation, confusion, and respiratory depression. Flumazenil is used to reverse the effects of benzodiazepines, not opioids. Option D - Stimulant overdose; administer IV diazepam: It is incorrect as stimulant overdose (e.g., cocaine or amphetamines) typically manifests with symptoms such as agitation, tachycardia, hypertension, and dilated pupils. The appropriate treatment for stimulant overdose does not involve IV diazepam, but rather supportive care and management of specific symptoms. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 55-year old female patient with a 1 cm thyroid nodule, palpable on physical exam, is referred to you. USG guided biopsy shows an 8 mm hypoechoic lesion, proves to be papillary thyroid cancer abutting on the trachea, without any evidence of local adenopathy. What would you recommend?
questions.stemHtml: A 55-year old female patient with a 1 cm thyroid nodule, palpable on physical exam, is referred to you. USG guided biopsy shows an 8 mm hypoechoic lesion, proves to be papillary thyroid cancer abutting on the trachea, without any evidence of local adenopathy. What would you recommend?

options.label: B
options.text: Repeat biopsy to rule out other process

questions.solution: Correct Option C - Lobectomy In this case, the patient has a 1 cm thyroid nodule that has been confirmed to be papillary thyroid cancer through biopsy. Furthermore, the lesion is abutting the trachea, which raises concerns about its proximity to important structures in the neck. Given the size of the lesion and its location, a lobectomy is an appropriate treatment choice. A lobectomy involves the removal of one lobe of the thyroid gland (either the right or left) and is often the initial surgical treatment for small, localized thyroid cancers. It helps ensure complete removal of the cancer while preserving thyroid function. Incorrect Options: Option A - Active surveillance with serial ultrasound: Active surveillance is an option for small thyroid nodules with indeterminate characteristics, especially when they are less than 1 cm in size and do not exhibit concerning features on ultrasound. However, in this case, the lesion has been confirmed as papillary thyroid cancer, which is a malignant tumor. Active surveillance is not appropriate for known thyroid cancer because the goal is to remove the cancer and prevent its spread. Option B - Repeat biopsy to rule out other processes: Since the biopsy has already confirmed the presence of papillary thyroid cancer, repeating the biopsy is unlikely to change the diagnosis. The management should focus on treating the confirmed cancer rather than seeking further confirmation. Option D - Total thyroidectomy: Total thyroidectomy involves the complete removal of the thyroid gland. While this may be necessary in some cases of thyroid cancer, it is often reserved for larger tumors, more aggressive types of thyroid cancer, or cases where there is evidence of cancer spreading beyond the thyroid gland. In this case, a lobectomy is more appropriate, as the cancer is small, localized, and has not shown evidence of local adenopathy or distant spread. @Neet_pg_bot

He also has a poor urinary stream, nocturia, and post-void dribbling. The vital signs and Laboratory tests were normal. On digital rectal examination, there is a palpable, hard, nodular prostate with an obliterated median sulcus. Ultrasound reports showed an enlarged prostate of weight 93 grams. His ratio of free: total PSA is estimated as 20%. The ultrasound of this patient is given below. What diagnosis does the doctor suspect in this case?
questions.stemHtml: A 66-year-old male presented to the local hospital with complaints of urinary retention with severe pain and burning sensation in the lower urinary tract since yesterday. He also has a poor urinary stream, nocturia, and post-void dribbling. The vital signs and Laboratory tests were normal. On digital rectal examination, there is a palpable, hard, nodular prostate with an obliterated median sulcus. Ultrasound reports showed an enlarged prostate of weight 93 grams. His ratio of free: total PSA is estimated as 20%. The ultrasound of this patient is given below. What diagnosis does the doctor suspect in this case?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Benign prostatic hyperplasia: It is a suspected case of benign prostatic hyperplasia due to urinary symptoms such as urinary retention, poor urinary stream, nocturia, and postvoid dribbling in the old male . Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is a benign enlargement of the prostate that occurs after 50 years, usually between 60 and 70 years. BPH affects both glandular epithelium and connective tissue stroma. It is involuntary hyperplasia due to disturbance of the ratio and quantity of circulating androgens and estrogens. •On digital rectal examination, a palpable prostate with smooth muscle hypertrophy is the typical finding of benign prostatic hyperplasia. •The free: total prostate-specific antigen ratio discriminates between prostate carcinoma and benign prostate hyperplasia. If it is < 18%, it is suggestive of carcinoma; if it is > 18 %, it suggests benign prostate hyperplasia, as it is 20% in this patient, indicating benign prostate hyperplasia. Incorrect Options: Option A - Tuberculous prostate: As there is no history and symptoms of tuberculosis, this disease does not correlate with the patient's condition. It is diagnosed by urine examination for ZN staining and culture of tubercle bacilli from the first morning urine sample. Option C - Acute prostatitis: It is the inflammation of the prostate due to any lower abdominal trauma or secondary to urinary tract infection. On palpation, there is a warm and tender prostate. Leukocytosis is the typical lab finding. Option D - Carcinoma of the prostate: The free: total ratio of PSA is the differentiating point between carcinoma and benign prostate hyperplasia. If it is > 18%, it is suggestive of benign prostate hyperplasia as this patient has a 20% ratio, so it excludes carcinoma of the prostate. @Neet_pg_bot

It is involuntary hyperplasia due to disturbance of the ratio and quantity of circulating androgens and estrogens.

•On digital rectal examination, a palpable prostate with smooth muscle hypertrophy is the typical finding of benign prostatic hyperplasia.

•The free: total prostate-specific antigen ratio discriminates between prostate carcinoma and benign prostate hyperplasia. If it is < 18%, it is suggestive of carcinoma; if it is > 18 %, it suggests benign prostate hyperplasia, as it is 20% in this patient, indicating benign prostate hyperplasia.       

Incorrect Options:

Option A - Tuberculous prostate:

  • It is diagnosed by urine examination for ZN staining and culture of tubercle bacilli from the first morning urine sample. 

Option C - Acute prostatitis:

  • It is the inflammation of the prostate due to any lower abdominal trauma or secondary to urinary tract infection.
  • On palpation, there is a warm and tender prostate. Leukocytosis is the typical lab finding.

Option D - Carcinoma of the prostate:

  • The free: total ratio of PSA is the differentiating point between carcinoma and benign prostate hyperplasia.
  • If it is > 18%, it is suggestive of benign prostate hyperplasia as this patient has a 20% ratio, so it excludes carcinoma of the prostate.

questions.stem: A 70-year old male underwent transurethral resection of the prostate for BPH under spinal anaesthesia. The patient is positioned in a lithotomy posture, and the surgery is done successfully. What is the most common complication that can occur because of the injury during surgery?
questions.stemHtml: A 70-year old male underwent transurethral resection of the prostate for BPH under spinal anaesthesia. The patient is positioned in a lithotomy posture, and the surgery is done successfully. What is the most common complication that can occur because of the injury during surgery?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Retrograde ejaculation: The transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) is the surgery done under spinal anesthesia. Retrograde ejaculation is the most common complication that occurs during surgery . It is due to injury of the internal urinary sphincter . The internal urinary sphincter is under the control of the L1 sympathetic ganglion . And ejaculation is under the sympathetic system. Incorrect Options: Option A - Erectile dysfunction: The erection is under the control of the parasympathetic system , so erectile dysfunction is not a complication of TURP. Option B - TURP syndrome: The complication after surgery due to continuous irrigation leads to dilutional hyponatremia called TURP syndrome. Option D - Urinary incontinence: It is the least common complication seen in < 1% of cases. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 33-year-old gentleman presents to the ER with a growing mass, distal to his right knee, biopsy from which revealed a high grade osteosarcoma, without any evidence of metastatic disease. He completes cisplatin and doxorubicin neo-adjuvant therapy for 3 cycles and then undergoes wide local excision. Path report shows negative margins. Review of the path report shows 25% viable tumor. What would you recommend ?
questions.stemHtml: A 33-year-old gentleman presents to the ER with a growing mass, distal to his right knee, biopsy from which revealed a high grade osteosarcoma, without any evidence of metastatic disease. He completes cisplatin and doxorubicin neo-adjuvant therapy for 3 cycles and then undergoes wide local excision. Path report shows negative margins. Review of the path report shows 25% viable tumor. What would you recommend ?

options.label: B
options.text: Continue with same regimen in the adjuvant setting

questions.answerText: Continue with same regimen in the adjuvant setting
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Continue with same regimen in the adjuvant setting : In this case: The patient received neoadjuvant chemotherapy with cisplatin and doxorubicin. Surgical resection was performed with wide local excision, and the margins were negative (clear), indicating that there was no visible tumor at the surgical margins. However, the pathologic examination of the surgical specimen revealed that 25% of the tumor tissue was still viable. This means that a significant portion of the tumor did not respond completely to chemotherapy. The recommended course of action in such cases, where there is a partial response to neoadjuvant chemotherapy but clear surgical margins, is to continue with the same chemotherapy regimen in the adjuvant setting. Adjuvant chemotherapy is administered after surgery to eliminate any remaining cancer cells and reduce the risk of recurrence. Incorrect Options: Option A - Clinical and radiographic surveillance: Surveillance without further treatment may not be sufficient in this case, as there is evidence of viable tumor remaining in the surgical specimen. Option C - Radiation therapy: Radiation therapy is not typically the first-line treatment for osteosarcoma but may be considered in certain cases, such as when there is inadequate surgical margin control or when the tumor is unresectable. In this case, the patient already had clear surgical margins, and the standard approach is to continue with chemotherapy in the adjuvant setting. Option D - Sorafenib: Sorafenib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor used in the treatment of some cancers, but it is not a standard treatment for osteosarcoma. The recommended approach in this case is to continue with chemotherapy. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Contraction of Cooper’s ligaments: Cooper ligaments provide shape and structure to the breast as they course from the overlying skin to the underlying deep fascia. Because these ligaments are anchored into the skin, infiltration of these ligaments by carcinoma commonly produces tethering, which can cause dimpling. Incorrect Options: Option A - Edema: Edema of the skin due to lymphatic obstruction by tumor emboli produces a peau d'orange appearance, not the skin dimpling. questions.answerText: Continue with same regimen in the adjuvant setting
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Continue with same regimen in the adjuvant setting : In this case: The patient received neoadjuvant chemotherapy with cisplatin and doxorubicin. Surgical resection was performed with wide local excision, and the margins were negative (clear), indicating that there was no visible tumor at the surgical margins. However, the pathologic examination of the surgical specimen revealed that 25% of the tumor tissue was still viable. This means that a significant portion of the tumor did not respond completely to chemotherapy. The recommended course of action in such cases, where there is a partial response to neoadjuvant chemotherapy but clear surgical margins, is to continue with the same chemotherapy regimen in the adjuvant setting. Adjuvant chemotherapy is administered after surgery to eliminate any remaining cancer cells and reduce the risk of recurrence. Incorrect Options: Option A - Clinical and radiographic surveillance: Surveillance without further treatment may not be sufficient in this case, as there is evidence of viable tumor remaining in the surgical specimen. Option C - Radiation therapy: Radiation therapy is not typically the first-line treatment for osteosarcoma but may be considered in certain cases, such as when there is inadequate surgical margin control or when the tumor is unresectable. In this case, the patient already had clear surgical margins, and the standard approach is to continue with chemotherapy in the adjuvant setting. Option D - Sorafenib: Sorafenib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor used in the treatment of some cancers, but it is not a standard treatment for osteosarcoma. The recommended approach in this case is to continue with chemotherapy. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: During ward rounds, you see a patient in the hospital for liver metastases, who presented with jaundice and had numerous liver and pulmonary metastases. Biopsy reveals a likely melanoma but further staining is needed. Which of the following stains is more specific to melanoma than other primary sites of disease?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - S100: S100 is a protein that is found in cells of neural crest origin, and it is expressed in melanocytes, which are the cells that give rise to melanoma. Immunohistochemical staining for S100 is a valuable diagnostic tool in identifying melanoma cells. It is particularly useful for confirming the diagnosis of melanoma when the histological features alone are not definitive. S100 staining is considered specific for melanoma and neuroectodermal tumors, as it is not typically expressed in most other primary malignancies. Therefore, when S100 staining is positive in a tumor biopsy, it strongly supports the diagnosis of melanoma. Incorrect Options: Option A - P63 / P40: P63 and P40 are markers commonly used to identify squamous cell carcinomas and are not specific to melanoma. They are often used to differentiate between different types of carcinomas, especially in cases where the histological appearance alone is insufficient for diagnosis. Option C - AE1/AE3: AE1 and AE3 are cytokeratin antibodies that are used to identify epithelial cells. They are not specific to melanoma and are typically used to differentiate epithelial tumors from other types of tumors. Option D - OCT3/4: OCT3/4 is an immunohistochemical marker used to detect germ cell tumors, particularly in the testes and ovaries. It is not specific to melanoma and is unrelated to the diagnosis of melanoma. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man has swelling in his left scrotum for two weeks, along with mild lower abdominal discomfort for four weeks. Physical exam reveals an enlarged testis, gynecomastia, and elevated serum markers. Imaging shows liver lesions and retroperitoneal lymph nodes. What are the risk factors for testicular tumors?
questions.stemHtml: A 34-year-old man has swelling in his left scrotum for two weeks, along with mild lower abdominal discomfort for four weeks. Physical exam reveals an enlarged testis, gynecomastia, and elevated serum markers. Imaging shows liver lesions and retroperitoneal lymph nodes. What are the risk factors for testicular tumors?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Klinefelter's syndrome: Testicular cancer is the most common cancer in men aged 20 to 40 years. Testicular tumors may be germ cell tumors or those that arise from stromal cells (Leydig or Sertoli cells). Germ cell tumors can be classified as either seminomatous or non-seminomatous. Seminoma constitutes more than 50% of all testicular tumors. Non-seminomatous germ cell tumors can be divided into the following histologic types: Embryonal carcinoma is a highly malignant tumor that occasionally invades cord structures. Yolk sac tumors are tumors with this component that secrete alpha-fetoprotein (AFP). Choriocarcinoma: Often produces human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG). This is a highly malignant tumor that metastasizes early by both the lymphatics and the bloodstream. Teratoma: These tumors contain more than one cell type with components derived from ectoderm, endoderm, and mesoderm. There are five well-established risk factors for testis cancer: White race Cryptorchidism Family history of testicular tumor, Personal history of testicular tumor Intratubular germ cell neoplasia (ITGCN) Klinefelter's syndrome is also a risk factor for testis cancer. Testicular cancer typically presents as testicular pain or a testicular mass. A scrotal ultrasound and serum tumor markers are the standard initial workup. Radical inguinal orchiectomy is the gold standard treatment for excision of the primary tumor. Pure seminoma is radiosensitive and can be treated with external beam radiation or a single dose of carboplatin. Non-seminomatous testis cancer can be cured with retroperitoneal lymph node dissection or chemotherapy. Seminomatous germ cell tumors generally have a better prognosis than non-seminomatous tumors. Incorrect Options: Option A - Extratubular germ cell neoplasia: Extratubular germ cell neoplasia is not a risk factor for testicular tumors. Option C - CA scrotum: It is a squamous cell carcinoma that may present as an ulcer with an everted edge. It was the first reported occupational cancer. It is not the risk factor for testicular tumors; instead, testicular tumors are the risk factor for the CA scrotum. Option D - Acute Epididymo-Orchitis (EDO): Acute Epididymo-Orchitis (EDO) is an acute inflammatory disease of the ipsilateral testes and epididymis. It is the risk factor for infertility, not for testicular tumors. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 4-year-old girl with a history of seizures comes to the emergency department because of headaches and more frequently occurring seizures. Physical examination shows patches of leathery-appearing and hypopigmented skin lesions scattered over her body. A subungual nodule is found on her left thumb. CT scan of the brain shows subependymal nodules, cortical foci with loss of the gray-white matter distinction, and a nodule partially obstructing the cerebral aqueduct. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the patient’s symptoms?
questions.stemHtml: A 4-year-old girl with a history of seizures comes to the emergency department because of headaches and more frequently occurring seizures. Physical examination shows patches of leathery-appearing and hypopigmented skin lesions scattered over her body. A subungual nodule is found on her left thumb. CT scan of the brain shows subependymal nodules, cortical foci with loss of the gray-white matter distinction, and a nodule partially obstructing the cerebral aqueduct. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the patient’s symptoms?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Giant-cell astrocytoma: Tuberous sclerosis (TS) is an autosomal dominant disorder with genetic heterogeneity. The brain tumors that are most commonly found in tuberous sclerosis are cortical tubers, subependymal nodules, or giant cell astrocytomas (SEGA). Image shows cortical tubers Giant-cell astrocytomas are low-grade neoplasms that appear to develop from the hamartomatous nodules in the brain. Ash-leaf spots, angiofibroma, and Shagreen patches are the most commonly seen dermatologic features. Though these tumors are benign, they often interfere with function causing seizures and other symptoms. Incorrect Options: Option A - Craniopharyngioma: Craniopharyngioma is a type of brain tumor derived from pituitary gland embryonic tissue in the suprasellar region that occurs most commonly in children but also in adults, ruling out this option. Initial symptoms may be bitemporal inferior quadrantanopia leading to bitemporal hemianopsia, as the tumor may compress the optic chiasm . Option B - Ependymoma: Ependymomas are tumours that usually arise in the ventricular system of the brain, including the central canal of the spinal cord. In the first two decades of life, they typically occur near the fourth ventricle, ruling out this option. Posterior fossa ependymomas manifest with hydrocephalus secondary to obstruction of the fourth ventricle. Option D - Medulloblastoma: This malignant embryonal tumor occurs most commonly in children. Medulloblastomas are typically located in the midline of the cerebellum. This tumor is often well-circumscribed and rapid growth may occlude the flow of CSF , leading to hydrocephalus. This option is thus ruled out. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Option B: Lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly are highly typical The above clinical presentation is suggestive of Aplastic anaemia. Lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly are highly atypical of aplastic anaemia. Aplastic anaemia: Aplastic anaemia is pancytopenia with bone marrow hypocellularity. Easy bruising, oozing from the gums, nose bleeds, heavy menstrual flow, and sometimes petechiae are noticed. Thrombocytopenia leads to small amounts of bleeding in the central nervous system resulting in intracranial or retinal haemorrhage. The following finds are supportive for aplastic anaemia: Mean corpuscular volume (MCV) is commonly increased. Reticulocytes are absent or few, and lymphocyte numbers may be normal or reduced. Bone marrow is hypocellular and shows mainly fat under the microscope. The severity of the disease is defined by the presence of 2 of 3 following parameters a) Absolute neutrophil count <500/μL b) Platelet count <20,000/μL c) Corrected reticulocyte count <1% (or absolute reticulocyte count <60,000/μL). Option A: Can be cured by Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation A bone marrow transplant also called a stem cell transplant, is the only standard cure for aplastic anaemia. Option C: Bleeding is the most common symptom Thrombocytopenia leads to small amounts of bleeding in the central nervous system resulting in intracranial or retinal haemorrhage. Option D: Immunosuppressants are given to cure the disease Immunosuppressant therapy with anti-thymocyte globulins and cyclosporin A is the first-line therapy for acquired aplastic anaemia in candidates unsuitable for bone marrow transplants @Neet_pg_bot

Aplastic anaemia:

  • Aplastic anaemia is pancytopenia with bone marrow hypocellularity.
  • Easy bruising, oozing from the gums, nose bleeds, heavy menstrual flow, and sometimes petechiae are noticed.
  • Thrombocytopenia leads to small amounts of bleeding in the central nervous system resulting in intracranial or retinal haemorrhage.
  • The following finds are supportive for aplastic anaemia:
    • Mean corpuscular volume (MCV) is commonly increased.
    • Reticulocytes are absent or few, and lymphocyte numbers may be normal or reduced.
    • Bone marrow is hypocellular and shows mainly fat under the microscope.

The severity of the disease is defined by the presence of 2 of 3 following parameters

a) Absolute neutrophil count <500/μL

b) Platelet count <20,000/μL

c) Corrected reticulocyte count <1% (or absolute reticulocyte count <60,000/μL).

Option A: Can be cured by Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation

  • A bone marrow transplant also called a stem cell transplant, is the only standard cure for aplastic anaemia.

Option C: Bleeding is the most common symptom

  • Thrombocytopenia leads to small amounts of bleeding in the central nervous system resulting in intracranial or retinal haemorrhage.

Option D: Immunosuppressants are given to cure the disease

  • Immunosuppressant therapy with anti-thymocyte globulins and cyclosporin A is the first-line therapy for acquired aplastic anaemia in candidates unsuitable for bone marrow transplants

questions.solution: Correct Option D- Decitabine plus venetoclax: The combination of a hypomethylating agent (HMA) like decitabine with a BCL2 inhibitor like venetoclax has emerged as an effective and well-tolerated treatment regimen for older adults with AML who are not candidates for intensive induction chemotherapy. Clinical trials have demonstrated good response rates with this combination, and it is becoming a standard option for many older patients with AML. This regimen is less intensive than traditional chemotherapy regimens, making it suitable for older patients like the one described who might not tolerate aggressive chemotherapy. Incorrect Options: Option A- Idarubicin plus low dose cytarabine (5+ 2): This is a less intensive form of chemotherapy than the traditional "7+3" regimen (cytarabine for 7 days and an anthracycline for 3 days). While it may be an option for some older adults with AML, the combination of decitabine and venetoclax is gaining favor due to its efficacy and tolerability. Option B- Ara-C 1g/m^2 for 3 cycles: High-dose cytarabine can be part of induction or consolidation treatment for AML in younger patients or those in excellent health. However, for older adults, especially those with an ECOG performance status of 1-2, this would be quite intensive and might be associated with significant toxicities. Option C- Idarubicin alone: Anthracyclines like idarubicin are traditionally used in combination with cytarabine as part of the induction regimen for AML. Using it alone would be unconventional and less likely to be effective. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: A 13-year-old girl is brought to the hospital complaining of fatigue, weakness, pale-coloured skin and shortness of breath. After proper evaluation, she is diagnosed with β-thalassemia major, and the physician advises frequent blood transfusion. Which of the following is the most appropriate drug that should be used to prevent iron overload in this patient?
questions.solution: Option B: Oral deferiprone Iron overload in frequent blood transfusion: During a blood transfusion, the body receives more iron, and as red cells break down over time, the iron in the haemoglobin is released. The body has no natural way to get rid of excess iron. So extra iron is stored in body tissues. That's why patients receiving frequent transfusions are at risk for iron overload. Excess iron usually deposits in the heart, pancreas, liver, and pituitary and causes organ damage. In β- thalassemia major , iron excess can occur due to repeated blood transfusions and massive hemolysis. So, thalassemia patients need to be treated with an iron-chelating agent to prevent iron overload. In this case, the chelating agent must be administered for a long time. Therefore, oral d eferiprone is preferred in this case. Other options Option A: Oral desferrioxamine The drug of choice for acute iron poisoning is desferrioxamine. It has to be administered parenterally. It is not effective by oral route. Option C: Intramuscular EDTA EDTA is also an iron-chelating agent, but it is mainly used to prevent clotting in a blood sample. It is not safe for use in humans longer than 5-7 days. Option D: Oral succimer It is used in acute lead poisoning to remove excess lead from the body. @Neet_pg_bot

Option B: Oral deferiprone

  • During a blood transfusion, the body receives more iron, and as red cells break down over time, the iron in the haemoglobin is released.
  • The body has no natural way to get rid of excess iron.
  • So extra iron is stored in body tissues. That's why patients receiving frequent transfusions are at risk for iron overload.
  • Excess iron usually deposits in the heart, pancreas, liver, and pituitary and causes organ damage.
  • In β-thalassemia major, iron excess can occur due to repeated blood transfusions and massive hemolysis.
  • So, thalassemia patients need to be treated with an iron-chelating agent to prevent iron overload.
  • In this case, the chelating agent must be administered for a long time. Therefore, oral deferiprone is preferred in this case.

Other options

Option A: Oral desferrioxamine

  • The drug of choice for acute iron poisoning is desferrioxamine.
  • It has to be administered parenterally.
  • It is not effective by oral route.

Option C: Intramuscular EDTA

  • EDTA is also an iron-chelating agent, but it is mainly used to prevent clotting in a blood sample.
  • It is not safe for use in humans longer than 5-7 days.

Option D: Oral succimer

  • It is used in acute lead poisoning to remove excess lead from the body.

questions.solution: Correct Option B- Argatroban: Argatroban: Argatroban is the drug of choice for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. questions.stemHtml: A 67-year-old male complained of generalized fatigue associated with difficulty breathing. On examination, pallor & gingival hypertrophy is noted. Initial investigations revealed hyperleukocytosis. Follow-up investigations showed leukostasis. This feature is most predominantly seen in which of the following disorders?
questions.solution: Option B: Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) Leukostasis (also called symptomatic hyperleukocytosis) is a medical emergency most commonly seen in patients with acute myeloid leukaemia. It is characterized by an extremely elevated blast cell count and symptoms of decreased tissue perfusion. The most common symptoms are dyspnea and hypoxia, usually accompanied by visual changes, headache, dizziness, confusion, somnolence and coma. Hyperleukocytosis and leukostasis syndrome are commonly associated with a complication of acute leukaemia (particularly myeloid leukaemia). It can occur when the peripheral blast cell count is >100,000/mL. The frequency of hyperleukocytosis is 13% in acute myeloid leukaemia (AML); however, leukostasis is rare in lymphoid leukaemia. Option A: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL) Leukostasis is seen primarily in myeloid leukaemia and is very rare in lymphoblastic leukaemia. Clinical features: Lymphoblast is proliferating so much → other lineages are suppressed Anemia Fatigue, Tiredness, and Pallor Depletion in neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils, and monocytes causes Recurrent infections Thrombocytopenia Option C: Chronic myelocytic leukaemia (CML) Leukostasis is seen very rarely in Chronic myeloid leukaemia CML has three phases (Chronic, Accelerated and Blast Crisis). Clinical features: Dragging sensation in the abdomen. Massive Splenomegaly (something pulling the abdomen down). Option D: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL) Leukostasis is seen primarily in myeloid leukaemia and is very rare in lymphocytic leukaemia. The earliest finding is a Fatigue. questions.stem: A 55-year-old male presents with red, violet, or purple discoloration of his toes upon exposure to heat. He also experiences itching all over his body during warm baths. Additionally, he reports occasional color changes in his lower limb extremities in response to cold temperatures. Which of the following conditions is most likely responsible for these symptoms?
questions.stemHtml: A 55-year-old male presents with red, violet, or purple discoloration of his toes upon exposure to heat. He also experiences itching all over his body during warm baths. Additionally, he reports occasional color changes in his lower limb extremities in response to cold temperatures. Which of the following conditions is most likely responsible for these symptoms?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Polycythemia vera: The clinical features described in the scenario are consistent with the diagnosis of Polycythemia vera. PV is a type of myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by the excessive production of RBCs independently from normal regulatory mechanisms. This condition presents with elevated hemoglobin and hematocrit levels, along with the possibility of increased WBC and/or platelet counts. PV often presents with symptoms related to increased blood viscosity, such as venous or arterial thrombosis (e.g., DVT, MI, stroke), pruritus, erythromelalgia (burning pain in the hands or feet), facial redness, visual disturbances, and headaches. Laboratory investigations include a complete blood count with differential count, blood smear examination, testing for the JAK2 V617F mutation in blood samples, and measuring serum erythropoietin (EPO) levels. Bone marrow examination, including microscopy and cytogenetics analysis, to assess for characteristic features of PV. Incorrect Options: Option B - Deep vein thrombosis (DVT): DVT is characterized by the formation of blood clots in deep veins, typically in the legs. It does not present with the specific symptoms of erythromelalgia, aquagenic pruritus, or Raynaud's phenomenon. Option C - Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE): SLE is an autoimmune disease that can affect multiple organs and systems. While it may present with various symptoms, it is not specifically associated with the described symptoms of erythromelalgia, aquagenic pruritus, or Raynaud's phenomenon. Option D - Peripheral artery disease (PAD): PAD involves narrowing or blockage of arteries, typically in the legs. It can cause symptoms such as leg pain, cramping, or decreased blood flow. However, it does not present with the specific features of erythromelalgia, aquagenic pruritus, or Raynaud's phenomenon. @Neet_pg_bot

  • It is an inherited blood disorder caused by a point mutation in the β-globin gene.
  • Mutant HbA is termed HbS (sickle haemoglobin).
  • Deoxygenated HbS polymerizes and causes sickling.
  • Pathogenesis: Low O2, high altitudes, dehydration, or acidosis triggers sickling.

    • Anaemia.
    • Painful swelling of hands and feet.

  • Proliferative sickle retinopathy (PSR) is the most severe ocular change in SCD.
  • Patients can present with acute chest syndrome (not pulmonary syndrome).
  • Acute chest syndrome is characterized by chest pain, tachypnea, fever, cough, and arterial oxygen desaturation., pulmonary bleeds are not seen.
  • Treatment: Hydroxyurea
  • Increases foetal haemoglobin and reduces sickling.
  • Beneficial effects on RBC hydration.
  • Reduces vascular wall adherence of sticky reticulocytes.

  • The HbA is mutated in sickle cell anaemia, and the mutant form is termed HbS.
  • Therefore, HbA is almost undetectable in this condition.

Option B: She may have retinopathy

  • The most severe ocular change in sickle cell disease is proliferative sickle retinopathy.

Option D: Hydroxyurea would help her

  • The most effective oral treatment for sickle cell anaemia is hydroxyurea.
  • It reduces sickling by increasing the amount of fetal haemoglobin.

questions.solution: Correct option: D - Subcutaneous epinephrine Type 2 brittle asthma are symptom-free patients developing sudden onset acute attacks of asthma requiring mechanical ventilation or even death These patients should ideally keep an auto-injector of epinephrine Type 1 brittle asthma is characterized by > 40% variation in PEFR for >50% of the time It is managed with long-acting β-agonists (LABA) + high-dose inhaled corticosteroids and oral steroids Long-term continuous subcutaneous infusion of β-2 agonists like terbutaline is also given in type 1 brittle asthma Management of type 2 brittle asthma: These patients are difficult to manage as they do not respond well to corticosteroids and the worsening of asthma does not reverse well with inhaled bronchodilators The most effective therapy is subcutaneous epinephrine, which suggests that the worsening is likely to be a localized airway anaphylactic reaction with edema Incorrect options: A, B and C Option A: asthma but not for type 2 as the worsening of asthma does not reverse with inhaled bronchodilators in these patients Option B: Allergy desensitization Allergy desensitization is an adjunctive controller treatment that can benefit a minority of patients with asthma and rhinitis driven by a specific aeroallergen (e.g., immunotherapy with house dust mite proteins) It is less effective for patients, such as this one, who have seasonal allergies but experience persistent asthma symptoms In the absence of appropriate asthma control, allergen challenges may cause asthma to worsen Option C:   • Type 2 brittle asthma are symptom-free patients developing sudden onset acute attacks of asthma requiring mechanical ventilation or even death
  • These patients should ideally keep an auto-injector of epinephrine
  • Type 1 brittle asthma is characterized by > 40% variation in PEFR for >50% of the time
  • It is managed with long-acting β-agonists (LABA) + high-dose inhaled corticosteroids and oral steroids
  • Long-term continuous subcutaneous infusion of β-2 agonists like terbutaline is also given in type 1 brittle asthma

Management of type 2 brittle asthma:

  • These patients are difficult to manage as they do not respond well to corticosteroids and the worsening of asthma does not reverse well with inhaled bronchodilators
  • The most effective therapy is subcutaneous epinephrine, which suggests that the worsening is likely to be a localized airway anaphylactic reaction with edema

Incorrect options: A, B and C

Option A: β-adrenergic agonist

  • LABA improve asthma control and reduce exacerbations when added to ICS, which allows asthma to be controlled at lower doses of corticosteroids
  • LABA can be used for type 1 brittle asthma but not for type 2 as the worsening of asthma does not reverse with inhaled bronchodilators in these patients

Option B: Allergy desensitization

  • Allergy desensitization is an adjunctive controller treatment that can benefit a minority of patients with asthma and rhinitis driven by a specific aeroallergen (e.g., immunotherapy with house dust mite proteins)
  • It is less effective for patients, such as this one, who have seasonal allergies but experience persistent asthma symptoms  
  • In the absence of appropriate asthma control, allergen challenges may cause asthma to worsen

Option C: Ipratropium bromide

  • Long-acting antimuscarinic agents (e.g., tiotropium) are indicated for step-up therapy in patients with poorly controlled persistent asthma, despite scheduled high-dose ICS-formoterol
  • They have no role in type 2 brittle asthma

questions.solution: Correct Option C - Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency : Alpha-1 antitrypsin (AAT) is a protease inhibitor that plays a crucial role in neutralizing elastase, an enzyme released by macrophages. In individuals with alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, there is a lack of functional AAT, leading to the unopposed activity of elastase. This imbalance can result in damage to the lung tissue, contributing to the development of bronchiectasis and panacinar emphysema. questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with a history of chronic bronchitis visits the doctor with a 1-month history of increasing dyspnea and coughing up viscous sputum. He inhaled a single pack of cigarettes every day for 20 years before quitting 5 years ago. Vital signs are; heart rate of 90/min, blood pressure of 130/90 mmHg, and respiratory rate of 30/min. Physical evaluation reveals symmetrically larger anteroposterior chest diameter and coarse crackles in the lower lung areas. The administration of a medication that effectively counteracts the effects of vagal activation on the airways is initiated. Which of the following medications was most likely initiated?
questions.stemHtml: A 50-year-old man with a history of chronic bronchitis visits the doctor with a 1-month history of increasing dyspnea and coughing up viscous sputum. He inhaled a single pack of cigarettes every day for 20 years before quitting 5 years ago. Vital signs are; heart rate of 90/min, blood pressure of 130/90 mmHg, and respiratory rate of 30/min. Physical evaluation reveals symmetrically larger anteroposterior chest diameter and coarse crackles in the lower lung areas. The administration of a medication that effectively counteracts the effects of vagal activation on the airways is initiated. Which of the following medications was most likely initiated?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Tiotropium: The antimuscarinic drug tiotropium treats asthma and chronic obstructive lung disease (COPD). This patient exhibits a persistent productive cough, a history of tobacco use, and greater anteroposterior lung girth coarse crackles on physical examination. All of these characteristics firmly point to a COPD diagnosis. Tiotropium specifically blocks the M3 muscarinic receptors in the airways, leading to the relaxation of bronchial smooth muscles and decreased bronchoconstriction. The competing binding of Tiotropium (and other long-acting parasympatholytics) to muscarinic receptors decreases the parasympathetic tone on the bronchioles, which prevents bronchoconstriction. Moreover, tiotropium also inhibits mucus secretion from goblet cells, leading to a reduction in airway obstruction. These results enhance lung efficacy and lessen the signs and symptoms of airway blockage. Incorrect Options: Option B - Fluticasone: Fluticasone and other inhaled glucocorticoids prevent the production of several cytokines, which has an anti-inflammatory impact. The transcription factor NF-B, which typically promotes the generation of inflammatory substances (such as TNF-), is inactivated by glucocorticoids in the nucleus. Despite being a component of the multimodal treatment for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, inhaled glucocorticoids do not counteract the effects of vagal activation on the airways. Option C- Montelukast: Anti-inflammatory drugs called anti-leukotrienes, such as montelukast, inhibit leukotriene receptors. (CysLT1). Leukotrienes cause bronchoconstriction and lung hyperreactivity. As a result, leukotriene receptor blockade causes bronchodilation. Montelukast is not recommended to treat chronic obstructive pulmonary disease despite reducing lung irritation. This drug has been shown to lessen the frequency of severe asthma episodes and is frequently prescribed to manage asthma. Additionally, montelukast does not counter the impacts of vagal activation on the airways. Option D - Albuterol: Beta 2-agonist, albuterol causes bronchodilation right away. It is used to treat acute bouts of asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease because it is a short-acting medication; it is not a component of long-term maintenance treatment. Additionally, the impacts of vagal activation on the airways are not countered by albuterol. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option D - Type 4 respiratory failure: Type 4 respiratory failure, also known as respiratory muscle pump failure, occurs due to underperfusion of respiratory muscles, particularly in conditions such as cardiogenic shock. In cardiogenic shock, decreased cardiac output leads to inadequate perfusion of respiratory muscles, resulting in respiratory distress. Management involves addressing the underlying cause of shock, such as with interventions like Impella or inotropes, and providing respiratory support with interventions like endotracheal intubation and intermittent positive pressure ventilation. Incorrect Options: Option A - Type 1 respiratory failure: Characterized by low arterial oxygen levels (hypoxemia) with normal or low arterial carbon dioxide levels (normocapnia or hypocapnia). questions.stem: A 24-year-old smoker presented to the emergency department with a non-productive cough, shortness of breath, and sudden onset pleuritic pain on the right side of the chest. On physical examination, the patient is afebrile and vitally stable. A chest examination showed diminished breath sounds on the right hemithorax. The physician ordered a chest X-ray, and a subsequent diagnosis of primary spontaneous pneumothorax (PSP) was made. Which of the following should be the appropriate management step for the above-mentioned case?
questions.stemHtml: A 24-year-old smoker presented to the emergency department with a non-productive cough, shortness of breath, and sudden onset pleuritic pain on the right side of the chest. On physical examination, the patient is afebrile and vitally stable. A chest examination showed diminished breath sounds on the right hemithorax. The physician ordered a chest X-ray, and a subsequent diagnosis of primary spontaneous pneumothorax (PSP) was made. Which of the following should be the appropriate management step for the above-mentioned case?
questions.solution: Correct option: C - Simple needle aspiration Primary spontaneous pneumothorax (PSP), a pneumothorax without underlying lung illness, is more common in young, slim males Pleural blebs or bullae that have burst are the typical culprits Most PSP cases are confirmed by an upright posteroanterior chest radiograph, which can accurately determine the size of the pneumothorax Needle aspiration should be performed on patients who have a primary spontaneous pneumothorax for the first time, who are hemodynamically stable, have a large pneumothorax (> 2-3 centimetres of air on a chest X-ray or > 15% of the hemithorax), have a progressive pneumothorax, or who are symptomatic with chest pain or dyspnea The patient can be discharged once the treatment is successful (< 2 millimetres of air in the chest X-ray and an improvement in the breathing pattern), with follow-up from 2 to 4 weeks Incorrect options: A, B and D Option A: Intermittent positive pressure ventilation (IPPV) Intermittent positive pressure ventilation (IPPV) is considered if the patient's respiratory status is in peril, is likely to become so, or when respiratory failure affects other bodily systems Option B: Closed drainage A chest tube is often employed when a pneumothorax cannot be resolved with needle aspiration Option D: Thoracotomy Surgery is indicated when an initial episode of PSP returns and causes chronic air leaks or a collapsed lung following the insertion of pleural drainage Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) for primary spontaneous pneumothorax has replaced open thoracotomy @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Correct option: C - Simple needle aspiration

  • Primary spontaneous pneumothorax (PSP), a pneumothorax without underlying lung illness, is more common in young, slim males
  • Pleural blebs or bullae that have burst are the typical culprits
  • Most PSP cases are confirmed by an upright posteroanterior chest radiograph, which can accurately determine the size of the pneumothorax
  • Needle aspiration should be performed on patients who have a primary spontaneous pneumothorax for the first time, who are hemodynamically stable, have a large pneumothorax (> 2-3 centimetres of air on a chest X-ray or > 15% of the hemithorax), have a progressive pneumothorax, or who are symptomatic with chest pain or dyspnea
  • The patient can be discharged once the treatment is successful (< 2 millimetres of air in the chest X-ray and an improvement in the breathing pattern), with follow-up from 2 to 4 weeks

Incorrect options: A, B and D

Option A: Intermittent positive pressure ventilation (IPPV)

  • Intermittent positive pressure ventilation (IPPV) is considered if the patient's respiratory status is in peril, is likely to become so, or when respiratory failure affects other bodily systems

Option B: Closed drainage

  • A chest tube is often employed when a pneumothorax cannot be resolved with needle aspiration

Option D: Thoracotomy

  • Surgery is indicated when an initial episode of PSP returns and causes chronic air leaks or a collapsed lung following the insertion of pleural drainage
  • Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) for primary spontaneous pneumothorax has replaced open thoracotomy

She reports a family history of asthma. On physical examination, there are bilateral expiratory wheezes heard throughout the chest. Which of the following is a characteristic of asthma?

options.label: A

questions.answerText: Asthma is characterized by airway obstruction that is partially or completely reversible with treatment.
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Asthma is characterized by airway obstruction that is partially or completely reversible with treatment: Asthma is a reversible condition that affects the airways of the lungs. During an asthma attack or exacerbation, the airways become inflamed, narrowed, and produce excessive mucus, leading to symptoms such as coughing, wheezing, chest tightness, and shortness of breath. In most cases, the airway obstruction in asthma is reversible , either spontaneously or with appropriate treatment. The degree of reversibility can vary from person to person and can depend on factors such as the severity and duration of the asthma attack, the individual's age and overall health, and the effectiveness of the treatment. However, in some cases, repeated and severe asthma attacks can lead to irreversible lung damage and a decline in lung function, known as airway remodelling. Airway remodelling is characterized by structural changes in the airways, such as increased smooth muscle and collagen deposition, which can lead to persistent airflow limitation and reduced response to bronchodilators. This irreversible lung damage is more likely to occur in individuals with severe and uncontrolled asthma, particularly those who smoke or have other risk factors such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).. Incorrect Options: Option B - Asthma is caused by irreversible damage to the airways, leading to permanent airway obstruction: Asthma is a reversible condition that can be managed with appropriate treatment. Irreversible damage to the airways can occur in other obstructive lung diseases like chronic bronchitis or emphysema. Option C - Asthma is caused by chronic bronchitis, leading to narrowing of the airways: Asthma and chronic bronchitis are two distinct diseases with different underlying pathophysiology. Chronic bronchitis is characterized by chronic inflammation and mucus production in the bronchi, leading to airway obstruction and impaired gas exchange. Option D - Asthma is caused by emphysema, leading to decreased lung elasticity: Asthma and emphysema are two distinct diseases with different underlying pathophysiology. Emphysema is a type of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) characterized by destruction of the alveolar walls, leading to loss of lung elasticity and impaired gas exchange. @Neet_pg_bot
