questions.stemHtml: What is the key feature distinguishing the disease in a 44-year-old man with involuntary facial grimacing and finger movements, reminiscent of his mother's symptoms that started around the same age and progressed to dancing movements, arm, and leg writhing, coma, and death, similar to his maternal grandfather's experience?

options.label: A
options.text: Degeneration of upper and lower motor neurons

options.label: B
options.text: Dopamine depletion and depigmentation of the substantia nigra

options.label: C
options.text: Increased number of trinucleotide repeats in a gene on chromosome 4

options.label: D
options.text: Neurofibrillary tangles and amyloid plaques in the cerebral cortex

questions.answerText: Increased number of trinucleotide repeats in a gene on chromosome 4
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Increased number of trinucleotide repeats in a gene on chromosome 4: This is a case of Huntington's disease. It is an autosomal dominant disorder It causes fatal, progressive degeneration and atrophy of the Striatum (Caudate nucleus and Putamen). It is characterised by an increased number of trinucleotide repeats (CAG) in the Huntington gene on the short arm of chromosome 4 . Incorrect Options: Option A - Degeneration of upper and lower motor neurons: Degeneration of the upper and lower motor neurons is characteristic of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. ALS initially presents with asymmetric weakness in hands, muscle cramping, and fasciculations, progressing to widespread muscle weakness and respiratory involvement. Variants include progressive muscular atrophy, primary lateral sclerosis, and bulbar ALS, each with distinct clinical features and prognoses. ALS can also involve cortical regions, leading to frontotemporal dementia, with genetic and pathological overlap between ALS and frontotemporal lobar degeneration. Option B - Dopamine depletion and depigmentation of the substantia nigra: Dopamine depletion and depigmentation of the substantia nigra are characteristic of Parkinson's disease. Clinical features include tremors, rigidity, akinesia/bradykinesia, and postural instability. Dementia is a common feature of late disease. Option D - Neurofibrillary tangles and amyloid plaques in the cerebral cortex: Neurofibrillary tangles and amyloid plaques are found in Alzheimer's disease . Alzheimer’s disease is the most common cause of dementia and movement disorders are not seen @Neet_pg_bot

  • It is characterised by an increased number of trinucleotide repeats (CAG) in the Huntington gene on the short arm of chromosome 4.

Incorrect Options:

Option A - Degeneration of upper and lower motor neurons:

  • Degeneration of the upper and lower motor neurons is characteristic of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
  • ALS initially presents with asymmetric weakness in hands, muscle cramping, and fasciculations, progressing to widespread muscle weakness and respiratory involvement.
  • Variants include progressive muscular atrophy, primary lateral sclerosis, and bulbar ALS, each with distinct clinical features and prognoses.
  • ALS can also involve cortical regions, leading to frontotemporal dementia, with genetic and pathological overlap between ALS and frontotemporal lobar degeneration.

Option B - Dopamine depletion and depigmentation of the substantia nigra:

  • Dopamine depletion and depigmentation of the substantia nigra are characteristic of Parkinson's disease.
  • Clinical features include tremors, rigidity, akinesia/bradykinesia, and postural instability.
  • Dementia is a common feature of late disease.

Option D - Neurofibrillary tangles and amyloid plaques in the cerebral cortex:

  • Neurofibrillary tangles and amyloid plaques are found in Alzheimer's disease.
  • Alzheimer’s disease is the most common cause of dementia and movement disorders are not seen

questions.stem: A second-year medical student learns about the regulation and function of prolactin in his endocrinology lecture. Which of the following dopaminergic pathway is involved in the secretion of prolactin?
questions.stemHtml: A second-year medical student learns about the regulation and function of prolactin in his endocrinology lecture. Which of the following dopaminergic pathway is involved in the secretion of prolactin?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Tuberoinfundibular: Prolactin is secreted by the anterior pituitary gland . Its secretion is inhibited by the production of dopamine by the tuberoinfundibular pathway of the hypothalamus . Decreased activity of this pathway results in increased production of prolactin. Thyroid-releasing hormone (TRH) can also stimulate the production of prolactin in conditions like primary or secondary hypothyroidism. Prolactin can inhibit its own secretion by increasing dopamine production from the hypothalamus. Functions of prolactin include: Stimulation of milk production Inhibition of ovulation (females) Inhibition of spermatogenesis (males) Dopamine agonists (cabergoline) are used to treat conditions in which prolactin excess (prolactinoma). Drugs like antipsychotics and antidepressants can decrease dopamine production and can result in an increase in prolactin levels. Incorrect Options: Option A - Mesocortical: Decreased activity of the mesocortical pathway results in negative symptoms like anergia and apathy. It is affected minimally by antipsychotics. Option B - Mesolimbic: Increased activity of the mesolimbic pathway results in positive symptoms like delusions and hallucinations. Antipsychotics have a marked effect on these pathways. Option C - Nigrostriatal: Decreased activity of nigrostriatal pathways results in extrapyramidal symptoms like dystonia and parkinsonism. It is notably affected by movement disorders. @Neet_pg_bot

Correct Option D - Tuberoinfundibular:

  • Prolactin is secreted by the anterior pituitary gland. Its secretion is inhibited by the production of dopamine by the tuberoinfundibular pathway of the hypothalamus. Decreased activity of this pathway results in increased production of prolactin.
  • Thyroid-releasing hormone (TRH) can also stimulate the production of prolactin in conditions like primary or secondary hypothyroidism.
  • Prolactin can inhibit its own secretion by increasing dopamine production from the hypothalamus.
  • Functions of prolactin include:
    • Stimulation of milk production
    • Inhibition of ovulation (females)
    • Inhibition of spermatogenesis (males)
  • Dopamine agonists (cabergoline) are used to treat conditions in which prolactin excess (prolactinoma).
  • Drugs like antipsychotics and antidepressants can decrease dopamine production and can result in an increase in prolactin levels.

Incorrect Options:

Option A - Mesocortical:

  • Decreased activity of the mesocortical pathway results in negative symptoms like anergia and apathy.
  • It is affected minimally by antipsychotics.

Option B - Mesolimbic:

  • Increased activity of the mesolimbic pathway results in positive symptoms like delusions and hallucinations.
  • Antipsychotics have a marked effect on these pathways.

Option C - Nigrostriatal:

  • Decreased activity of nigrostriatal pathways results in extrapyramidal symptoms like dystonia and parkinsonism.
  • It is notably affected by movement disorders.

questions.stemHtml: A woman presents 4 months after delivery of a healthy full-term newborn. She complains that she has not had her periods since delivery. She is exclusively breastfeeding her infant. A urine pregnancy test is negative. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of her amenorrhea?
questions.solution: Correct Option: Option A: Prolactin-induced inhibition of GnRH Lactational amenorrhea: The physiological basis of anovulation and amenorrhea is elevated levels of serum prolactin associated with suckling. Elevated serum prolactin levels suppress the normal pattern of pulsatile release of GnRH and hence, LH and prevent the normal growth of follicles. With the cessation of breastfeeding, the pulsatile pattern of LH returns to normal, sensitivity to estrogen-negative feedback declines, follicle growth can continue, and ovulation will occur. Incorrect Options: Option B: Prolactin-induced stimulation of FSH Prolactin inhibits the release of GnRH and thus reduces LH and FSH secretion, resulting in anovulation and amenorrhea. Option C : I nadequate breastfeeding Adequate and exclusive breastfeeding is important for the occurrence of this amenorrhea and resulting contraception. Suckling during lactation reduces GnRH secretion, which leads to a decrease in the levels of LH secreted from the pituitary and estrogen levels. It lasts for 3 to 6 months or longer. Three criteria, must be met to ensure adequate protection from an unplanned pregnancy: Amenorrhea Fully or nearly fully breastfeeding (no interval of >4–6 hours between breastfeeds) <6 months postpartum. Option D : Oxytocin-induced inhibition of FSH Oxytocin does not stimulate or inhibit the release of FSH. The two main physical functions of oxytocin are stimulating uterine contractions in labor and childbirth to stimulate contractions of breast tissue to aid in lactation after childbirth. @Neet_pg_bot

Lactational amenorrhea:

  • With the cessation of breastfeeding, the pulsatile pattern of LH returns to normal, sensitivity to estrogen-negative feedback declines, follicle growth can continue, and ovulation will occur.

Incorrect Options:

Option B: Prolactin-induced stimulation of FSH

  • Prolactin inhibits the release of GnRH and thus reduces LH and FSH secretion, resulting in anovulation and amenorrhea.

Option C: Inadequate breastfeeding

  • Adequate and exclusive breastfeeding is important for the occurrence of this amenorrhea and resulting contraception.
  • Suckling during lactation reduces GnRH secretion, which leads to a decrease in the levels of LH secreted from the pituitary and estrogen levels.
  • It lasts for 3 to 6 months or longer.
  • Three criteria, must be met to ensure adequate protection from an unplanned pregnancy:
    •  Amenorrhea
    •  Fully or nearly fully breastfeeding (no interval of >4–6 hours between breastfeeds)
    •  <6 months postpartum.

Option D: Oxytocin-induced inhibition of FSH

  • Oxytocin does not stimulate or inhibit the release of FSH.
  • The two main physical functions of oxytocin are
    • stimulating uterine contractions in labor and childbirth
    • to stimulate contractions of breast tissue to aid in lactation after childbirth.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old female presents to the emergency department with complaints of nausea, vomiting, and confusion. Her laboratory results reveal serum sodium (Na+) concentration of 118 mmol/L, serum osmolality of 255 mOsm/kg, and urine osmolality of 600 mOsm/kg. The patient has a history of bilateral adrenal incidentalomas that were incidentally discovered on a previous abdominal CT scan. The endocrinology team is consulted, and further laboratory workup revealed a Plasma renin activity (PRA): 0.2 ng/mL/h (normal range 0.2-2.9 ng/mL/h), Plasma aldosterone concentration (PAC): 5 ng/dL (normal range <10 ng/dL), Morning cortisol level: 18 mcg/dL (normal range 4-22 mcg/dl). An ACTH stimulation test is performed, and the results show a peak cortisol level of 20 mcg/dL (normal response >20 mcg/dL). Based on these findings, which of the following is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
questions.stemHtml:
A 55-year-old female presents to the emergency department with complaints of nausea, vomiting, and confusion. Her laboratory results reveal serum sodium (Na+) concentration of 118 mmol/L, serum osmolality of 255 mOsm/kg, and urine osmolality of 600 mOsm/kg. The patient has a history of bilateral adrenal incidentalomas that were incidentally discovered on a previous abdominal CT scan. The endocrinology team is consulted, and further laboratory workup revealed a
Plasma renin activity (PRA): 0.2 ng/mL/h (normal range 0.2-2.9 ng/mL/h),
Plasma aldosterone concentration (PAC): 5 ng/dL (normal range &lt;10 ng/dL),
Morning cortisol level: 18 mcg/dL (normal range 4-22 mcg/dl).
An ACTH stimulation test is performed, and the results show a peak cortisol level of 20 mcg/dL (normal response &gt;20 mcg/dL).
Based on these findings, which of the following is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH): Euvolumic low serum sodium concentration, hypo-osmolality, and high urine osmolality are consistent with SIADH . SIADH causes include head trauma/CNS disorders, ectopic ADH (eg, small cell lung cancer), exogenous hormones (eg, vasopressin, desmopressin, oxytocin), lung disease, and drugs (eg, SSRIs, carbamazepine, cyclophosphamide). SIADH will result in free water reabsorption in the kidneys by increasing aquaporins in the distal convoluted tubules and collecting ducts. Excess free water reabsorption causes low serum osmolality (less than 275 mOsm/kg) and hyponatremia. Incorrect Options: Option B - Cerebral salt wasting syndrome (CSWS): A rare condition that is characterised by hyponatremia and dehydration. It is typically seen in patients with central nervous system (CNS) injury or surgery and is associated with excess secretions of natriuretic peptides. It causes hypovolemic, hypotonic hyponatremia, although the mechanism is poorly understood. Classically, its onset occurs within 10 days of an inciting event within the central nervous system (particularly subarachnoid haemorrhage) or neurosurgical procedure. Severe symptoms are treated with hypertonic saline and fludrocortisone. Option C - Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison’s disease): It is caused by damage to the adrenal gland, leading to decreased production of cortisol and aldosterone. The laboratory findings of low PRA and PAC levels are consistent with adrenal insufficiency, but the normal morning cortisol level and ACTH stimulation test results make this diagnosis less likely. Option D - Pseudohyponatremia: It is a laboratory artefact that occurs due to a dilutional effect when there is hyperlipidemia or hyperproteinemia . Asymptomatic laboratory artifact falsely indicating hyponatremia when sodium has not been reduced or diluted Due to very high amounts of protein or lipids in the plasma (e.g., hyperlipidemia , multiple myeloma ), which then alter the plasma water concentration Clinical features may include: Pancreatitis Diabetic ketoacidosis Obstructive jaundice Multiple myeloma In this case, the patient’s laboratory findings are consistent with true hyponatremia, making pseudo-hyponatremia an unlikely diagnosis. @Neet_pg_bot

  • SIADH causes include head trauma/CNS disorders, ectopic ADH (eg, small cell lung cancer), exogenous hormones (eg, vasopressin, desmopressin, oxytocin), lung disease, and drugs (eg, SSRIs, carbamazepine, cyclophosphamide).
  • SIADH will result in free water reabsorption in the kidneys by increasing aquaporins in the distal convoluted tubules and collecting ducts.
  • Excess free water reabsorption causes low serum osmolality (less than 275 mOsm/kg) and hyponatremia.

Incorrect Options:

Option B - Cerebral salt wasting syndrome (CSWS):

  • A rare condition that is characterised by hyponatremia and dehydration. It is typically seen in patients with central nervous system (CNS) injury or surgery and is associated with excess secretions of natriuretic peptides.
  • It causes hypovolemic, hypotonic hyponatremia, although the mechanism is poorly understood.
  • Classically, its onset occurs within 10 days of an inciting event within the central nervous system (particularly subarachnoid haemorrhage) or neurosurgical procedure.

The laboratory findings of low PRA and PAC levels are consistent with adrenal insufficiency, but the normal morning cortisol level and ACTH stimulation test results make this diagnosis less likely.

questions.stem: Which of the following actions of insulin on adipose tissue is incorrect?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following actions of insulin on adipose tissue is incorrect?

options.label: B
options.text: Insulin increases the uptake of free fatty acids into fat cells.

options.label: D
options.text: Insulin promotes the breakdown of triglycerides into free fatty acids.

questions.answerText: Insulin promotes the breakdown of triglycerides into free fatty acids.
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Insulin promotes the breakdown of triglycerides into free fatty acids: Insulin has various actions on adipose tissue, primarily aimed at promoting the storage of energy in the form of triglycerides. However, insulin does not promote the breakdown of triglycerides into free fatty acids. The correct action is the inhibition of hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL) activity. Incorrect Options : Option A - Insulin stimulates lipoprotein lipase (LPL) activity: Insulin indeed stimulates the activity of lipoprotein lipase, an enzyme that breaks down triglycerides into free fatty acids for uptake into fat cells. Option B - Insulin increases the uptake of free fatty acids into fat cells: Insulin promotes the uptake of free fatty acids into fat cells by stimulating the activity of GLUT-4 transporters, which allow glucose and free fatty acids to enter the cell. Option C - Insulin inhibits hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL) activity: Hormone-sensitive lipase is responsible for breaking down triglycerides into free fatty acids. Insulin inhibits the activity of HSL, preventing the breakdown of triglycerides and promoting their storage. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option D - Aging: This patient presented with symptoms of acromegaly and laboratory investigations confirmed the diagnosis. Acromegaly occurs due to excessive production of growth hormone. Growth hormone is secreted by the anterior pituitary gland. It is also known as somatotropin. Its effects are mediated via somatomedins (insulin-like growth factors). The most significant among these is somatomedin C (insulin-like growth factor1). Growth hormone via IGF-1 performs many essential functions in the body, including: Promotion of deposition of protein in the tissues Enhancing utilization of fat for energy Decreasing utilization of carbohydrates Stimulation of growth of cartilage and bones The secretion of the growth hormone is in a pulsatile manner. Its rate of secretion changes depending on numerous factors. The secretion of GH is increased by the following stimuli: Decreased blood glucose Decreased blood free fatty acids Increased blood amino acids Starvation Stress Exercise Deep sleep Ghrelin The secretion of GH is decreased by the following stimuli: Increased blood glucose Increased blood free fatty acids Aging Obesity Somatostatin Exogenous growth hormone Somatomedins Incorrect Options: Option A - Trauma: Trauma can increase the release of growth hormone from the anterior pituitary gland. This help in the metabolic response to the injury. Option B - Ghrelin: Ghrelin can increase the release of growth hormone from the anterior pituitary gland. Somatomedins and somatostatin decrease the release of GH. Option C - Exercise: Exercise can increase the release of growth hormone from the anterior pituitary gland. Aging results in a decrease in the release of GH. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Correct Option D - Aging:

  • This patient presented with symptoms of acromegaly and laboratory investigations confirmed the diagnosis. Acromegaly occurs due to excessive production of growth hormone.
  • Growth hormone is secreted by the anterior pituitary gland. It is also known as somatotropin.
  • Its effects are mediated via somatomedins (insulin-like growth factors). The most significant among these is somatomedin C (insulin-like growth factor1). 
  • Growth hormone via IGF-1 performs many essential functions in the body, including:
    • Promotion of deposition of protein in the tissues
    • Enhancing utilization of fat for energy
    • Decreasing utilization of carbohydrates
    • Stimulation of growth of cartilage and bones
  • The secretion of the growth hormone is in a pulsatile manner. Its rate of secretion changes depending on numerous factors. 
  • The secretion of GH is increased by the following stimuli:
    • Decreased blood glucose
    • Decreased blood free fatty acids
    • Increased blood amino acids
    • Starvation
    • Stress
    • Exercise
    • Deep sleep
    • Ghrelin
  • The secretion of GH is decreased by the following stimuli:
    • Increased blood glucose
    • Increased blood free fatty acids
    • Aging
    • Obesity
    • Somatostatin
    • Exogenous growth hormone
    • Somatomedins

Incorrect Options:

Option A - Trauma:

  • Trauma can increase the release of growth hormone from the anterior pituitary gland.
  • This help in the metabolic response to the injury.

Option B - Ghrelin:

  • Ghrelin can increase the release of growth hormone from the anterior pituitary gland.
  • Somatomedins and somatostatin decrease the release of GH.

Option C - Exercise:

  • Exercise can increase the release of growth hormone from the anterior pituitary gland.
  • Aging results in a decrease in the release of GH.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old female with type 1 diabetes mellitus presents to the endocrinology clinic for a routine follow-up visit. She is on insulin and reports experiencing episodes of postprandial hyperglycemia. On further evaluation, it was decided to add a medication that specifically target postprandial hyperglycemia in her treatment regimen. The drug is an analog of a certain hormone that is released by?
questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old female with type 1 diabetes mellitus presents to the endocrinology clinic for a routine follow-up visit. She is on insulin and reports experiencing episodes of postprandial hyperglycemia. On further evaluation, it was decided to add a medication that specifically target postprandial hyperglycemia in her treatment regimen. The drug is an analog of a certain hormone that is released by?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Beta cells of the pancreas: In the case where the drug used to target postprandial hyperglycemia is pramlintide, it is an analog of amylin. Amylin is a hormone co-secreted with insulin by the beta cells of the pancreas. It functions alongside insulin to regulate blood glucose levels. Pramlintide injected just before a meal slows gastric emptying and suppresses glucagon but does not alter insulin levels and promotes satiety, all of which contribute to the control of postprandial (after-meal) blood glucose levels. By mimicking amylin's actions, pramlintide can help reduce postprandial hyperglycemia in individuals with type 1 or type 2 diabetes mellitus. Incorrect Options: Option A - Alpha cells of the pancreas: Alpha cells of the pancreas secrete glucagon, a hormone that works in opposition to insulin. Glucagon raises blood glucose levels by stimulating the liver to release stored glucose. However, the drug mentioned in the scenario, pramlintide, is an analogue of amylin, which is secreted by beta cells, not alpha cells. Option C - Delta cells of the pancreas: Delta cells of the pancreas secrete somatostatin, a hormone that inhibits the release of insulin and glucagon. While somatostatin plays a regulatory role in glucose metabolism, it is not the hormone mimicked by pramlintide, which is used to target postprandial hyperglycemia. Option D - F cells of the pancreas: F cells, also known as pancreatic polypeptide (PP) cells, secrete pancreatic polypeptide. Pancreatic polypeptide plays a role in regulating pancreatic exocrine function and may have some influence on appetite regulation. However, it is not the hormone mimicked by pramlintide for targeting postprandial hyperglycemia. @Neet_pg_bot

Lab tests show low hemoglobin levels and elevated MCV. Peripheral smear shows the following findings. What is the mechanism of action of the drug responsible for the patient's condition?
questions.stemHtml: A 60-year-old man with type 2 diabetes complains of weakness, fatigue, and shortness of breath. During a physical examination, the patient appears pale and has conjunctival pallor. Lab tests show low hemoglobin levels and elevated MCV. Peripheral smear shows the following findings. What is the mechanism of action of the drug responsible for the patient's condition?

options.label: A
options.text: Inhibition of hepatic glucose production and glucose absorption

questions.answerText: Inhibition of hepatic glucose production and glucose absorption
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Inhibition of hepatic glucose production and glucose absorption: The presence of macrocytic anemia and elevated MCV suggests a potential deficiency in vitamin B12 or folate, leading to impaired red blood cell production and enlargement. The Howell-Jolly bodies seen in the peripheral smear indicate a potential dysfunction of the spleen. The antidiabetic drug that inhibits hepatic glucose production and glucose absorption is a biguanide, specifically metformin. While metformin does not directly cause macrocytic anemia or Howell-Jolly bodies, long-term use of metformin has been associated with reduced levels of vitamin B12 and possibly impaired spleen function. Incorrect Options: Option B - Stimulation of insulin secretion: This mechanism of action is associated with sulfonylureas. Sulfonylureas work by stimulating insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells. It is associated with hypoglycemia and weight gain. Option C - Inhibition of glucagon release: This mechanism of action is associated with dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) inhibitors, which degrades incretin hormones like glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), resulting in increased insulin secretion and decreased glucagon release, associated with angioedema, urticarial, and immune-mediated dermatologic effects. Option D - Enhancement of renal glucose excretion: This mechanism of action is associated with sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors. SGLT2 inhibitors work by inhibiting glucose reabsorption in the kidneys, leading to increased glucose excretion in the urine. It is associated with urinary and genital infections, polyuria, and hyperkalemia. @Neet_pg_bot

Which of the following statements is true regarding anti-reflux surgery in this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 42-year-old female patient comes to your OPD to discuss further management of GERD. She was initially tried on H2-blocker therapy and had an initial response that was then lost. She was subsequently started on PPIs twice daily and has had inadequate symptom improvement. Recent VOGD demonstrates persistent esophagitis but no Barrett’s esophagus or mass lesion. pH studies confirm the presence of GERD. She is frustrated by her remaining symptoms, which have begun to affect her ability to exercise and sleep and her ability to swallow various foods safely. She has also been experiencing worsening regurgitation lately, which was confirmed by a manometry study last month. She asks whether surgery will lead to symptom improvement. Which of the following statements is true regarding anti-reflux surgery in this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Anti-reflux surgery will eliminate her risk of esophageal cancer.

options.label: B
options.text: Anti-reflux surgery has been shown to improve symptoms in patients with regurgitation.

options.label: C
options.text: Endoluminal antireflux procedures are as effective as anti-reflux surgery without the associated complications of surgery.

options.label: D
options.text: Since she has no evidence of metaplasia or dysplasia on EGD, she is not a candidate for antireflux surgery at this time.

questions.answerText: Anti-reflux surgery has been shown to improve symptoms in patients with regurgitation.
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Anti-reflux surgery has been shown to improve symptoms in patients with regurgitation: Multiple studies have shown that while anti-reflux surgery does help with symptoms in certain patients, it does not alter an individual’s risk for esophageal cancer. Fundoplication should be reserved for patients with proven regurgitation using esophageal manometry studies. Endoscopic anti-reflux procedures including radiofrequency augmentation of the lower esophageal sphincter and endoscopic suturing of the sphincter have not been proven to result in long-term symptom control. Studies have shown that at 3 years after the procedures, patients continued to need medical therapy or a fundoplication procedure. Anti-reflux surgery is contraindicated in patients with metaplasia or dysplasia since it can affect treatment options in case of progression to cancer. questions.stem: Which of the following parasitic infections is usually associated with occult blood in stool?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following parasitic infections is usually associated with occult blood in stool?
questions.solution: Correct Option D- Strongyloides: TRUE: Occult blood in stool is associated with hookworm or Strongyloides infection. Strongyloides stercoralis enters the human host when skin contacts the larvae through infected soil usually contaminated with feces. The parasite can live for up to 5 years in humans, eventually burrowing into the mucosa of the duodenum as adults. Eggs produced by the adult female pass in the feces. Eosinophilia points to a parasite infection. The adult worm migrates to the small bowel and can cause duodenitis, leading to epigastric pain that is aggravated by food ingestion. Patients complain of diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, and anorexia. Pulmonary manifestations can include wheezing, dyspnea, and hemoptysis. Patients may complain of a dry cough, and chronic infection may result in recurrent pulmonary symptoms that are suggestive of bacterial pneumonia. Diagnosis is usually made by detection of characteristic larvae in stool or by serology. Incorrect Options: Option A-Coccidiosis: FALSE: Coccidiosis is associated with chronic tropical diarrhea. Option B- Giardia: FALSE: Giardia is associated with a malabsorption syndrome. Option C-Isospora belli: FALSE: Isospora belli is a parasite that causes chronic tropical diarrhea. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 4-week-old boy is brought to the emergency department with the complaint of vomiting for 2 weeks. According to the mother, vomitus consists of milk and is non bilious without blood. He has had small spit-ups since birth, but for the last few days, he has been vomiting forcefully after every feed and his condition is deteriorating . His appetite is normal and he always seems hungry. The infant was born to a 27-year-old primigravida via normal vaginal delivery who did not seek prenatal care. On examination, his temperature is 37.2°C (98.9°F), blood pressure is 90/70 mmHg, heart rate is 120/min, and respiratory rate is 26/min. The baby appears dehydrated and abdominal examination reveals visible gastric peristaltic waves and a palpable “olive-shaped” mass in the right upper quadrant of the abdomen. Which of the following is the surgery of choice for this patient’s presentation?
questions.stemHtml: A 4-week-old boy is brought to the emergency department with the complaint of vomiting for 2 weeks. According to the mother, vomitus consists of milk and is non bilious without blood. He has had small spit-ups since birth, but for the last few days, he has been vomiting forcefully after every feed and his condition is deteriorating . His appetite is normal and he always seems hungry. The infant was born to a 27-year-old primigravida via normal vaginal delivery who did not seek prenatal care. On examination, his temperature is 37.2°C (98.9°F), blood pressure is 90/70 mmHg, heart rate is 120/min, and respiratory rate is 26/min. The baby appears dehydrated and abdominal examination reveals visible gastric peristaltic waves and a palpable “olive-shaped” mass in the right upper quadrant of the abdomen. Which of the following is the surgery of choice for this patient’s presentation?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Ramstedt’s pyloromyotomy: This patient's presentation, including forceful vomiting, feeling hungry despite vomiting, visible gastric peristaltic waves, and a palpable "olive-sized" mass in the right upper quadrant of the abdomen, is consistent with hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis: Pyloric stenosis is a thickening of the pylorus (the muscle between the stomach and the intestines) that causes severe and forceful vomiting in the first few months of life. It is also called infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. Clinical features: Vomiting after feeding at 4-8 weeks of age. The baby may vomit forcefully, ejecting breast milk or formula up to several feet away (forceful projectile vomiting). Vomitus is usually nonbloody and nonbilious. Persistent hunger: babies who have pyloric stenosis often want to eat soon after vomiting Dehydration Changes in bowel movements Poor weight gain Causes: The causes of pyloric stenosis are unknown, but genetic and environmental factors might play a role. Risk factors: Risk factors for pyloric stenosis include: Sex: more often in boys, especially firstborn boys , than in girls. Race: more common in whites of Northern European ancestry, less common in black people and rare in Asians. Premature birth : more common in babies born prematurely than in full-term babies. Family history: Pyloric stenosis develops in about 20% of male descendants and 10% of female descendants of mothers who had the condition. Smoking during pregnancy: doubles the risk of pyloric stenosis. Early antibiotic use : Babies given certain antibiotics like erythromycin in the first weeks of life have an increased risk of pyloric stenosis. In addition, babies born to mothers who took certain antibiotics (like macrolides) in late pregnancy may have an increased risk of pyloric stenosis. Bottle-feeding : Some studies suggest that bottle-feeding rather than breastfeeding increases the risk of pyloric stenosis. Most of the people who participated in these studies used formula feeds rather than breast milk, so it isn't clear whether the increased risk is related to formula feeds or the mechanism of bottle feeding. Electrolyte abnormality seen: hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria in case of severe dehydration. (Large amounts of vomitus lead to loss of HCl and K + with the kidney in turn compensating by reabsorbing more Na + and HCO3- in exchange of H+ to maintain the intravascular volume and pH causing the above mentioned abnormality.) Diagnosis: Abdominal ultrasound: It is the gold standard for diagnosing infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. Management: Resuscitation by I.V fluids along with correction of electrolyte levels, particularly potassium Fluid of choice: Normal Saline The treatment of choice after resuscitation is surgery. Surgery is needed to treat pyloric stenosis. The procedure (Ramstedt’s pyloromyotomy) is often scheduled on the same day as the diagnosis. If the baby is dehydrated or has an electrolyte imbalance, he or she will have a fluid replacement before surgery. A pyloromyotomy, or Ramstedt's procedure, is a procedure where the muscle of the pylorus of the stomach is divided to allow normal stomach emptying. Incorrect Options: Option A - Duodenostomy: Tube duodenostomy involves the insertion of a small feeding tube through the duodenal stump to encourage the formation of a controlled duodeno-cutaneous fistula. It is done for the management of difficult duodenal stumps in certain cases of partial gastrectomy or duodenal ulcers. Option B - Billroth Type-I procedure: The Billroth I operation is a type of reconstruction after a partial gastrectomy in which the pylorus of the stomach is anastomosed to the duodenum. It is most commonly performed in the management of peptic ulcers and gastric carcinoma. Option C - KASAI operation: The Kasai procedure involves removing the blocked bile ducts and gallbladder and replacing them with a segment of the child's own small intestine. This segment of the intestine is sewn to the liver and functions as a new extrahepatic biliary system . It is performed in biliary atresia. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 2-week-old male child is brought to the emergency department with complaints of abdominal distension, incessant crying, and failure to take feeds. What does the marked white arrow in the x-ray show?
questions.stemHtml: A 2-week-old male child is brought to the emergency department with complaints of abdominal distension, incessant crying, and failure to take feeds. What does the marked white arrow in the x-ray show?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Necrotizing enterocolitis: This patient's symptoms of abdominal pain, reduced oral intake, and abdominal distension, together with the radiological findings of air in the bowel wall, are indicative of necrotizing enterocolitis. Pneumatosis intestinalis is the specific term for the presence of gas within the wall of the small or large intestine. It involves subserosa, submucosa, and rarely, muscularis layer. Most common site: Jejunum > ileocecal region > colon Pneumatosis in neonates is usually associated with necrotizing enterocolitis In gross appearance, the cysts resemble cystic lymphangiomas or hydatid cysts On the histologic section, the involved portion has a honeycomb appearance On plain films, pneumatosis intestinalis appears as radiolucent areas within the bowel wall, as shown by the arrow. The radiolucency may be linear or curvilinear or appear as grape-like clusters or tiny bubbles. Incorrect Options: Option A - Ileal perforation: Small bowel (SB) perforation is an acute pathological condition resulting from a discontinuity of the small bowel wall secondary to trauma, typhoid fever, and congenital conditions in this age group with subsequent leakage of intestinal gas and contents into the peritoneal cavity. Abdominal x-ray shows free air under the diaphragm. The x-ray shown in the question shows air in the bowel wall and not under the diaphragm. Option C - Meconium ileus: Meconium ileus refers to a neonatal bowel obstruction of the distal ileum due to an abnormally thick and impacted meconium. It is usually a manifestation of cystic fibrosis. Plain radiographs are non-specific and may show dilated bowel loops proximal to the impaction. Classically, there is a paucity or absence of air-fluid levels and a "bubbly" appearance of the distended intestinal loops on radiographs. Option D - Colonic aganglionosis: Hirschsprung disease is characterized by aganglionosis (absence of ganglion cells) in the distal colon and rectum. X-ray findings are primarily those of a bowel obstruction. The affected bowel is of smaller caliber ; thus, depending on the length of the segment affected, a variable amount of colonic distension is present. @Neet_pg_bot

  • Ileocecal tuberculosis is the most common site of gastrointestinal tuberculosis, which in turn is the third most common site of extrapulmonary tuberculosis. questions.stem: A 30-year-old female with a history of dysmenorrhea and pelvic pain presents with dyschezia, diarrhea, and bloating. You suspect rectovaginal endometriosis as the cause of her symptoms, which are more pronounced during menses. Which of the following is true?
questions.stemHtml: A 30-year-old female with a history of dysmenorrhea and pelvic pain presents with dyschezia, diarrhea, and bloating. You suspect rectovaginal endometriosis as the cause of her symptoms, which are more pronounced during menses. Which of the following is true?

options.label: A
options.text: Rectal endoscopic ultrasound is the first-line study for evaluation of rectovaginal endometriosis.

options.label: B
options.text: A double-contrast barium enema is the initial recommended imaging test for suspected endometriosis.

options.label: C
options.text: Sigmoidoscopy and colonoscopy are the most useful studies for the identification of bowel endometriosis.

options.label: D
options.text: Definitive therapy is hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy and removal of extrapelvic lesions that are symptomatic

questions.answerText: Definitive therapy is hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy and removal of extrapelvic lesions that are symptomatic
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Definitive therapy is hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy and removal of extrapelvic lesions that are symptomatic: A trial of medical therapy is usually the initial line of treatment in patients with endometriosis, but surgical treatment is definitive. Since rectovaginal and bowel endometriosis coexist with other diseases, definitive treatment is hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy with removal of rectovaginal lesions. Incorrect Options: Option A - Rectal endoscopic ultrasound is the first-line study for evaluation of rectovaginal endometriosis: Transvaginal ultrasound is the first study used for evaluation of rectovaginal endometriosis because rectal endoscopic ultrasound is associated with more discomfort and the need for sedation. After identification of rectovaginal endometriosis, rectal endoscopic ultrasound can be used to determine the distance from anal junction and the depth of infiltration when evaluating the need for surgery. Option B - A double-contrast barium enema is the initial recommended imaging test for suspected endometriosis: Double-contrast barium enema may reveal information about partial bowel obstruction, but the information is not specific to endometriosis, so it is not useful for evaluation or initial diagnosis. Option C - Sigmoidoscopy and colonoscopy are the most useful studies for the identification of bowel endometriosis: Sigmoidoscopy and colonoscopy have limited utility since endometrial lesions do not usually penetrate the mucosa. @Neet_pg_bot

Since rectovaginal and bowel endometriosis coexist with other diseases, definitive treatment is hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy with removal of rectovaginal lesions.

Incorrect Options:

Option A - Rectal endoscopic ultrasound is the first-line study for evaluation of rectovaginal endometriosis: Transvaginal ultrasound is the first study used for evaluation of rectovaginal endometriosis because rectal endoscopic ultrasound is associated with more discomfort and the need for sedation. After identification of rectovaginal endometriosis, rectal endoscopic ultrasound can be used to determine the distance from anal junction and the depth of infiltration when evaluating the need for surgery.

Option B - A double-contrast barium enema is the initial recommended imaging test for suspected endometriosis: Double-contrast barium enema may reveal information about partial bowel obstruction, but the information is not specific to endometriosis, so it is not useful for evaluation or initial diagnosis.

Option C - Sigmoidoscopy and colonoscopy are the most useful studies for the identification of bowel endometriosis: Sigmoidoscopy and colonoscopy have limited utility since endometrial lesions do not usually penetrate the mucosa.
